tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Determine the region of convergence by using exponential weighting to identify the set of $s$-plane values for which a signal's Laplace-transform integral converges.

blocks.text:
The object to recognize is the **region of convergence**.
For a given signal $x(t)$, the ROC is the set of complex values $s$ where the Laplace integral exists and is finite.

Take one complex point $s=\sigma+j\omega$ and test directly whether the integral is finite. The action is: separate the kernel into a magnitude term and a phase term, then use $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$, so convergence is controlled by the real exponent factor and the signal tail, not by oscillation alone.

Then define the ROC as all $s$ values that pass that convergence test. That means the same rule applies point-by-point in the $s$-plane: collect every $\sigma+j\omega$ that makes the integral finite into one explicit set.

Result: the ROC is the full set of $s$ that satisfy the inequality. In the next sections, turn this test into a condition on $\sigma$ and then reinterpret that condition as a geometric $s$-plane region.

example_content.example_prompt: Compute whether the Laplace transform converges for $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ at $s=-1+j\,3$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the Laplace test form $X(s)=\int_0^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. For a single-point check, substitute the candidate $s$ value directly and test whether the resulting integral value is finite.
Separate the exponential terms. Since $|e^{-j3t}|=1$, the oscillatory factor $e^{-j3t}$ does not change magnitude, so convergence is controlled by $\int_0^{\infty}e^{-t}\,dt$.
Result: the integral is finite, so the Laplace transform converges at $s=-1+j3$. In the lesson rule form, $\sigma=-1$ and the condition $\sigma>-2$ is true.

sections.section_title: Converting a Convergence Test into a Condition on $\sigma$

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, rewrite the convergence result as a condition on $\sigma$ for all $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue now is to convert a single-point outcome into a reusable inequality. Start from the same weighted kernel and isolate the part of the exponent that drives magnitude.
Use $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$ so only the real-exponential factor sets tail behavior. This means convergence is equivalent to the real exponent on $e^{-2t}e^{-\sigma t}=e^{-(2+\sigma)t}$ being negative.
So for all $s=\sigma+j\omega$, the ROC is the half-plane defined by $\sigma>-2$. Boundary is the vertical line Re{$s$}$=-2$, and the valid side is the right side of that line.

sections.section_title: Marking the Region of Convergence in the $s$-Plane

image_slots.image_description: Plot the complex $s$-plane with $\sigma$ on the horizontal axis and $j\omega$ on the vertical axis. Draw the vertical boundary line at $\sigma=-2$ and clearly shade the half-plane where $\sigma>-2$ (the right side). Label the boundary as excluded for this strict inequality.

example_content.example_prompt: Given condition $\mathrm{Re}\{s\}> -2$, show the ROC on the $s$-plane and mark the boundary.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: the algebraic result is $\sigma>-2$ for the signal $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$. The action is to map this inequality into the $s$-plane and mark every admissible $s$ point.
The shaded region is the right half-plane. It is the set of points with $\sigma>-2$, so the $j\omega$ axis is inside this ROC since $\sigma=0$ satisfies the inequality.

Interpretation for the next step: a ROC condition written as $\mathrm{Re}\{s\}>a$ always means shade away from the left boundary side and keep the boundary line labeled as excluded unless an equality condition is explicitly stated.

sections.section_title: Checking Whether the Fourier-Transform Slice Is Included in the Region of Convergence

example_content.example_prompt: For ROC $\mathrm{Re}\{s\}> -2$, decide whether the Fourier-transform slice $s=j\omega$ is included.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a direct membership test: use the derived ROC inequality and the slice identity $s=j\omega$ to test whether one point on the $s$-plane is inside.
Step 1 is to convert the slice to a real-part test: $s=j\omega \iff \sigma=0$. That gives a single scalar value for the condition.
Step 2 is to check the ROC inequality with this value: substitute into $\mathrm{Re}\{s\}>-2$ and evaluate $0>-2$, which is true.
Result: the Fourier-transform slice is included in the ROC, so the original signal has a valid $X(j\omega)$ interpretation for this ROC inequality.

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Determine the region of convergence by using exponential weighting to identify the set of $s$-plane values for which a signal's Laplace-transform integral converges.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, test whether $X(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-3t}e^{-st}\,dt$ converges at $s=-2+j4$.

choice_blocks.text: Converges, because $\sigma=-2$ and $\sigma>-3$.
Diverges, because $\sigma=-2$ and $\sigma<-3$.
Diverges, because $|s|>3$ makes the exponential grow.
Converges conditionally but not absolutely, because $e^{-j4t}$ oscillates.
Diverges, because the test should use $\omega=4$ and $4>-3$.

questions.correct_answer: Converges, because substituting $s=-2+j4$ leaves the magnitude controlled by $e^{-t}$, so $\sigma=-2>-3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor $e^{-j4t}$ has magnitude $1$, so convergence is controlled by $\int_0^{\infty}e^{-t}\,dt$, which is finite. Thus the transform converges at this $s$ value.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{t}u(t)$, test whether $X(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{t}e^{-st}\,dt$ converges at $s=j2$.

choice_blocks.text: Converges, because $\omega=2$ and the imaginary part creates oscillation.
Diverges, because $\sigma=0$ and the required condition is $\sigma>1$.
Converges, because $\sigma=0$ and $0>-1$.
Converges conditionally but not absolutely, because $e^{-j2t}$ oscillates.
Diverges only if $|s|<1$, so this point converges because $|j2|=2$.

questions.correct_answer: Diverges, because substituting $s=j2$ leaves the magnitude controlled by $e^{t}$, so $\sigma=0$ does not satisfy $\sigma>1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The oscillatory factor $e^{-j2t}$ has magnitude $1$, so the tail behaves like $\int_0^{\infty}e^{t}\,dt$, which is not finite. Therefore the Laplace transform diverges at $s=j2$.

sections.section_title: Converting a Convergence Test into a Condition on $\sigma$

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-4t}u(t)$, convert the convergence requirement into the inequality on $\sigma$ that defines the ROC for $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>-4$
$\sigma<-4$
$\sigma\ge -4$
$\omega>-4$
$\sigma>4$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude-relevant exponential is $e^{-4t}e^{-\sigma t}=e^{-(4+\sigma)t}$. The tail converges only when the exponent coefficient is negative, so $-(4+\sigma)<0$, which gives $\sigma>-4$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{3t}u(t)$, rewrite the convergence test as a condition on $\sigma$ for all $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>3$
$\sigma<3$
$\sigma\ge 3$
$\omega>3$
$\sigma>-3$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The product $e^{3t}e^{-st}$ has magnitude $e^{(3-\sigma)t}$ because $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$. Convergence requires $3-\sigma<0$, so the ROC condition is $\sigma>3$.

sections.section_title: Marking the Region of Convergence in the $s$-Plane

image_slots.image_description: Plot the complex $s$-plane with horizontal real axis labeled $\sigma$ and vertical imaginary axis labeled $j\omega$. Draw a dashed vertical boundary line at $\sigma=-1$ and shade the open right half-plane $\sigma>-1$. Mark the boundary as excluded and do not write the ROC inequality in the image.

Plot the complex $s$-plane with horizontal real axis labeled $\sigma$ and vertical imaginary axis labeled $j\omega$. Draw a dashed vertical boundary line at $\sigma=2$ and shade the open left half-plane $\sigma<2$. Mark the boundary as excluded and do not write the ROC inequality in the image.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram marks a ROC on the $s$-plane. Which description matches the shaded region?

choice_blocks.text: Excluded vertical boundary at $\sigma=-1$, with the half-plane $\sigma>-1$ shaded.
Excluded vertical boundary at $\sigma=-1$, with the half-plane $\sigma<-1$ shaded.
Excluded vertical boundary at $\sigma=1$, with the half-plane $\sigma>1$ shaded.
Horizontal boundary at $\omega=-1$, with the half-plane $\omega>-1$ shaded.
Only the boundary line $\sigma=-1$ is included; no half-plane is part of the ROC.

questions.correct_answer: Excluded vertical boundary at $\sigma=-1$, with the half-plane $\sigma>-1$ shaded.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A condition of the form $\mathrm{Re}\{s\}>a$ means $\sigma>a$, so the boundary is the vertical line $\sigma=a$ and the shaded side is to the right. The strict inequality excludes the boundary line.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram marks a ROC on the $s$-plane. Which condition matches the shaded region?

choice_blocks.text: $\mathrm{Re}\{s\}>2$; vertical boundary at $\sigma=2$ with the right half-plane shaded.
$\mathrm{Re}\{s\}<2$; vertical boundary at $\sigma=2$ with the left half-plane shaded.
$\mathrm{Re}\{s\}\le 2$; vertical boundary at $\sigma=2$ included with the left half-plane shaded.
$\mathrm{Re}\{s\}<-2$; vertical boundary at $\sigma=-2$ with the left half-plane shaded.
$\omega<2$; horizontal boundary at $\omega=2$ with the lower half-plane shaded.

questions.correct_answer: $\mathrm{Re}\{s\}<2$; vertical boundary at $\sigma=2$ with the left half-plane shaded.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The real coordinate in the $s$-plane is $\sigma=\mathrm{Re}\{s\}$. Shading left of the vertical line $\sigma=2$ represents $\sigma<2$, and the dashed boundary shows that equality is excluded.

sections.section_title: Checking Whether the Fourier-Transform Slice Is Included in the Region of Convergence

prompt_blocks.text: For a signal whose ROC is $\sigma>1$, decide whether the Fourier-transform slice $s=j\omega$ is included.

choice_blocks.text: Yes; the slice is included because $0>1$ is true.
No; the slice is not included because $s=j\omega$ gives $\sigma=0$ and $0>1$ is false.
Yes; the slice is included for all values of $\omega$ because the ROC condition should be checked with $\omega$.
No; the slice is excluded only because the ROC should be tested with $\sigma=\omega$.
Yes; every right-half-plane ROC automatically includes the Fourier-transform slice.

questions.correct_answer: No; since $s=j\omega$ has $\sigma=0$ and $0>1$ is false, the Fourier-transform slice is not included in the ROC.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The Fourier-transform slice is the line $s=j\omega$, so its real part is $\sigma=0$. Substitute that value into the ROC inequality.
Because $\sigma=0$ does not satisfy the ROC, the $j\omega$ axis is not included and $X(j\omega)$ does not exist for this ROC.

prompt_blocks.text: For a signal whose ROC is $\sigma<0$, decide whether the Fourier-transform slice $s=j\omega$ is included.

choice_blocks.text: Yes; the slice is included because $0<0$ is true on the boundary.
Yes; the slice is included because strict ROC boundaries still contain the boundary line.
No; $s=j\omega$ gives $\sigma=0$, and $0<0$ is false.
No; the test should use $\omega<0$, so only negative frequencies converge.
Yes; the slice is included because the ROC points toward the left half-plane.

questions.correct_answer: No; $s=j\omega$ means $\sigma=0$, and $0<0$ is false, so the Fourier-transform slice is outside the ROC.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The inclusion test uses the real part of $s=j\omega$, not the value of $\omega$. On that slice, $\sigma=0$.
Since the inequality is strict, the boundary line $\sigma=0$ is not included. Therefore the Fourier-transform slice is not included in the ROC.
